item.title: Malware uses LLMs to rank victims by how much they're worth (124 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-ai-model-driven-victim-prioritization-in-the-volta-infostealer/, See on Hacker News

Saturday, October 31, 2026 08:00

  • VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
  • If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. 
  • This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. 

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.” 

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions 

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash 

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output 

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities 

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.  

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated. 

Deployment model 

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.  

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.  

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.  

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures 

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. 

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. 

Conclusions 

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement. 

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.  

Sample details

57ef4242666d78c50df145b34023df564f0fad38812d6a580e66433d427e2279

item.title: Prospero: A new coding harness for a more civilized age (139 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/, See on Hacker News

October 31, 2026

nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/

I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now. The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular, higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued to popen(). This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own: Prospero. It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear ImGui docking interface. It uses around two orders of magnitude fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features.

Dark mode aficionados are covered, too:

Note that Prospero comes with no model providers built-in. You’re expected to supply that yourself, such as with llama.cpp, a workplace on-prem model, OpenRouter, Anthropic API, OpenAI API, etc. (You can’t use your Claude subscription.)

For those unfamiliar with coding harnesses: In a chat interface you and the AI take turns writing messages to each other. A coding harness extends this concept, allowing an AI to “talk” to tools offered by the harness. Tools “reply” with their outputs. A tool might read or write a file, or run a shell command. An AI will go from tool call to tool call on its own, looping on the results. Such an AI is called an agent. Occasionally the AI will send you a message to inform you of progress or to ask a question, and the chat interface is still there.

Some harnesses, including Prospero, allow agents to spawn subagents to do their bidding, to work in parallel or keep their context clean. That is, to not fill their working memory with subtasks. Agents can message one another and coordinate on tasks. Given SSH access to another machine, or over plain WSL, Prospero can deploy a headless copy of itself to other hosts so that agents can operate on those systems. The Professional Edition embeds engines for combinations of x86/x86-64 and ARM64 on macOS, Windows, and Linux. The Windows x86 engine even works on Windows XP, and can play solitaire and minesweeper if you ask.

The last is because Prospero is one of the few harnesses with desktop control capabilities. If your model supports vision — any any model worth using does — then it can “see” your desktop and interact with it. It can click, type, and drag to test and debug GUI applications live without a specialized, per-app MCP assist.

This headless engine is why no TUI is necessary. The harness engine runs on the headless system, and the UI runs on your desktop or laptop. With a little extra setup, the harness to run fully independently of the GUI, so that it will continue without the GUI system attached — re-attachable later.

Because Prospero is so lean, it may be the only harness that can drive a fuzz campaign, particularly on a headless system, without the Linux OOM killer targeting the memory-gobbling harness rather than the out-of-control fuzz target that triggered it. So many times I’ve checked back in on a fuzz campaign hours later, to find nothing was accomplished because the harness process is gone.

(Why have an agent run a fuzz campaign? Because it can fix discovered bugs on the fly and keep the campaign going! It’s a no brainer.)

Configuration

The configuration lives at ~/.config/prospero/prospero.ini. Easy to edit. No JSON, thank goodness. Check it into source control, copy-paste it. All the usual benefits. Alternatively, the Settings page can reach every setting from the GUI, so you don’t have to edit the INI by hand. INI files can also include each other, not just naming file system paths but URLs:

include = https://example.com/prospero.ini

The idea is to allow a live shared or managed configuration. Includes by URL are restricted in what they can set, with a hard rule against anything which might appear in shell command. Some trust is still required, as a configuration can extract an environment variable by using it as an API key and supplying an endpoint it controls.

Prospero fetches a model list and other parameters like context size from the endpoint, but you might want to tweak it. A typical configuration may look like:

model = falstaff/Qwen3.8-27B

[endpoint falstaff]
url = http://falstaff.local/
key = env:FALSTAFF_API_KEY

[model Qwen3.8-27B]
edit_format = replace
template.reasoning_effort = medium

[model Qwen3.8-27B-xhigh]
like = Qwen3.8-27B
template.reasoning_effort = xhigh

[web]
search = searxng
url = https://search.example.com/
key = env:EXAMPLE_API_KEY

Passive rendering

The ImGui paradigm typically uses active rendering, redrawing on vsync like a video game. This is appropriate in some contexts, like interfaces within video games. Less so for mostly-static text-oriented UIs, such as a coding harness. Instead Prospero uses passive rendering with settle frames to finish animations before going idle. When there’s nothing to do, Prospero does nothing. It won’t chew on the GPU while the agent is waiting on a build.

Never wait forever

An annoyance with most other harnesses is how easily they get stuck. I set a long-running task, go to sleep, and in the morning find the harness hung on a trivial issue two hours into the night, wasting the rest. Therefore Prospero prime design principle: Never wait forever. Every operation has a deadline. This decision influences everything. If you’re not there to grant a requested permission, the agent will get a denial by timeout and must do without. To assist, Prospero will raise a system toast when an agent requires your attention so that you’re less likely to miss it if you’re attending.

The harness itself plows through intermittent errors, trying its best to drive the agent to complete its task. All network requests have timeouts, and watchdogs prevent endless waiting. Agent mailboxes are bounded.

Shell commands that hit their timeout convert to asynchronous background commands. The agent can continue to wait on them, with a timeout, and so will be woken at regular intervals to decide if it should continue.

The one exception is Plan mode, where it waits indefinitely after offering a plan or requesting clarification (ask_user tool). It’s expected that a user is attending to the agent during Plan mode.

No stray processes

The harnesses I’ve used have improved, but another regular annoyance earlier this year was agents starting processes that never get cleaned up. An agent kicks off a parallel build, hits a timeout because it was too optimistic, the build “stops” by killing a piece of the build system. But actually the build continues anyway, at least in part. The agent tries again, and now two builds are going, interfering with each other, making a mess and bringing my system to its knees.

For awhile I was wary of letting agents run builds in certain harnesses, which is a terrible outcome. You want agents to close the loop and iterate independently. A human in the loop is like putting a ball and chain on the agent, giving up most of its advantages.

Prospero promoting a synchronous timeout to an asynchronous task is a huge improvement on its own, but there’s an additional principle at play: The whole process tree lives and dies together. When a command is stopped, it stops. This is trivial on Windows, though few harnesses seem to take advantage of it. It’s more difficult on macOS and Linux, but Prospero follows through.

Built-in self-help

Like every harness, Prospero supports skills, a pre-packaged set of instructions on how to accomplish some task (“I know kung fu.”). Prospero contains a skill on itself and can read its built-in documentation. Ask the agent how to do or configure something in Prospero, and the agent can only answers your question, it can provide a hyperlink taking you to the relevant place in the UI. It can also edit your prospero.ini and reload it, to configure things on your behalf. This is not unique to Prospero, but I’m not aware of any harness doing this nearly as well.

Choose your shell

On Windows, Prospero is designed to work well with w64devkit, and will prefer its shell if available. Models designed for coding know w64devkit out-of-the-box, so these tools are complementary. Of course you’re not locked into that shell, and you can freely choose a different default shell. But Prospero is a rare harness where you can change shells mid session. Sometimes PowerShell is more suited to the task, so you can pick it out of the dropdown. The agent is informed of the change, and told about known quirks (i.e. “this is an old Bash!”). On macOS you can switch between bash and zsh.

The usual features

Prospero has the usual sorts of features you can expect from an advanced shell. It can use Git worktrees, including subagent worktrees, so that agents can share a repository. It speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It can search the web (if you allow). You can start side chats that share context, realized as subagents. You can fork sessions.

For now there is no built-in terminal or editor. Instead Prospero will open an external terminal or editor of your choosing. I’d rather use Vim than a built-in notepad.exe-equivalent. With Ctrl+G you can edit your prompt in an external editor.

Like all harnesses, the permissions system will not stop a malicious agent. Agents are writing and running programs on your computer, and so can ultimately access everything the harness can access. Permissions are about gently reminding the agent of your wishes, and catching simple mistakes. More like, “Whoa there, stay within the project” or, “Do not control my desktop at this time.” If you want to lock an agent out, you have to restrict the harness itself, putting it in a container or on a Raspberry Pi, at the usual cost of inconvenience or cutting off useful resources.

I’m really excited about Prospero, and I honestly feel it’s one of the best coding harnesses available. It’s how such tools ought to be built, but until now nobody else stepped up to do it. It would take a video to do it justice, and maybe I’ll do that sometime, but that’s currently outside my experience.

Most of the audience for my projects are hobbyists, even w64devkit. But if Prospero goes beyond me and my little circle, I expect most users would be professionals building commercial products. I’ve also invested more than just my time into this project — already true for w64devkit, even more true with Prospero. So while it’s an open source project, I’ve split it into two tiers:

  • Community Edition: the build you find on GitHub at no cost. It has no built-in headless engines, so remote deployments are limited. Plus a little nag text to remind you you’re on the Community Edition. Suited for hobbyists.

  • Professional Edition: Pay a nominal fee, get a DRM-free download with free updates. All the headless engines are built in so you can push remote deployments and remote sessions on other systems at the press of a button. A serious feature for professionals.

Windows and macOS builds are code-signed in both cases (some of the cost). If Prospero is useful for you professionally, even without the remote deployment feature, you’re still encouraged to buy a copy to support my ongoing costs!

item.title: We Took over ChatGPT Accounts (219 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.parameter.ai/labs/we-found-a-gap-at-openai, See on Hacker News

In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

Technical walkthrough

It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

The message that should not have worked

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.

This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run.

The next step was an iframe using srcdoc, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

The response began like this:

Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.

Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.

We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.

The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:

  1. A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page.
  2. A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.

The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.

An alert was not enough

At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:

GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2

This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.

Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.

What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

  1. MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
  2. The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
  3. That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity.

The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

  • A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission.
  • Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML.
  • Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame.
  • CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.

This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.

Timeline

DateEvent
October 13, 2026Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code.
October 14Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript.
October 16Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click.
October 17Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh.
October 18Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program.
October 19Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof.
October 21OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1.
October 22OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated.
October 23CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained.
October 26OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.

Technical notes

The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.

The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:

Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:

createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

The parser and CSP transition. The innerHTML operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed srcdoc caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted www.youtube.com in script-src-elem.

The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with ;void consumed the error object appended by the endpoint.

For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with toString(), double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. URLSearchParams then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside <script src>, and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's srcdoc attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters.

The authenticated read. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers:

Authorization: Bearer <victim token>
ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account>
Accept: application/json

The primary requests were:

GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true

Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers.

Key takeaways

  • Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender.
  • postMessage receivers must authenticate both event.origin and event.source before accepting state-changing instructions.
  • HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe.
  • The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as chatgpt.com, it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert.
  • Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone.

The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.

item.title: Switch Lowering in GCC (158 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://xoranth.net/gcc-switch/, See on Hacker News

Switch lowering in GCC

2024-01-14

Introduction

We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?

In this post, I'll focus on gcc. All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the -O3 optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.

I've also slightly edited gcc code and removed certain assertions for brevity.

Examples

Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers x and val. Depending on the value of x, it calls a corresponding function (f0, f1, and so forth) with val as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 1:
            return f1(val);
        case 2:
            return f2(val);
        case 3:
            return f3(val);
        case 4:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.

Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 97:
            return f0(val);
        case 98:
            return f1(val);
        case 99:
            return f2(val);
        case 100:
            return f3(val);
        case 101:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact:
	lea	eax, [rdi-97]
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	mov	edi, esi
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is.

Through experimentation, we find that gcc considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per case label.

In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact_7(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 7:
            return f1(val);
        case 14:
            return f2(val);
        case 21:
            return f3(val);
        case 34:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact_7:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 34
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L3
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4

But this other function is expanded as a tree of comparisons:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int sparse_8(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 8:
            return f1(val);
        case 16:
            return f2(val);
        case 24:
            return f3(val);
        case 40:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

sparse_8:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 16
	je	.L2
	jle	.L10
	cmp	eax, 24
	je	.L7
	cmp	eax, 40
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f4
.L10:
	test	eax, eax
	je	.L4
	cmp	eax, 8
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f1
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L4:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f3
.L2:
	jmp	f2

Here's the comparison tree visualized for clarity:

A couple of observations:

  1. We've only tried equally spaced values so far. Can the compiler identify transformations that are profitable on a subset of all cases?
  2. So far each case led to a different result. What if we had different cases with the same result?
  3. The switch in sparse_8 could be simplified by dividing x by eight before the jump. Interestingly, gcc doesn't find this simplification.

Let's dig into 1. and 2.

Outliers

Altering our first example by including an outlier value shows that the compiler is able to recognize dense subsets of cases.

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);
int f5(int val);

int outlier(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            return f0(val);
        case 2:
            return f1(val);
        case 3:
            return f2(val);
        case 4:
            return f3(val);
        case 5:
            return f4(val);
        case 100:
            return f5(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

outlier:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 5
	jg	.L2
	test	eax, eax
	jle	.L1
	cmp	eax, 5
	ja	.L4
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L6[0+rax*8]]
.L6:
	.quad	.L4
	.quad	.L4
	.quad	.L9
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L5
.L2:
	cmp	eax, 100
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f5
.L7:
	jmp	f3
.L5:
	jmp	f4
.L9:
	jmp	f1
.L8:
	jmp	f2
.L4:
	jmp	f0
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

The compiler emits a branch for case 100, but emits a jump table for case 1 through 5.

Contiguous

In our examples so far, each case statement lead to a different code block. Let's test what happens when multiple case labels invoke the same function.

int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);
int f5(int val);

int blocks_2(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:  case 1:  case 2:  case 3:
            return f1(val);
        case 21:  ...  case 24:
            return f2(val);
        case 42:  ...  case 45:
            return f3(val);
        case 63:  ...  case 66:
            return f4(val);
        case 84:  ...  case 87:
            return f5(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

blocks_2:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 45
	jg	.L2
	cmp	eax, 41
	jg	.L3
	cmp	eax, 3
	jg	.L4
	test	eax, eax
	js	.L1
	jmp	f1
.L2:
	cmp	eax, 66
	jg	.L8
	cmp	eax, 62
	jle	.L1
	jmp	f4
.L4:
	sub	eax, 21
	cmp	eax, 3
	ja	.L1
	jmp	f2
.L8:
	sub	eax, 84
	cmp	eax, 3
	ja	.L1
	jmp	f5
.L3:
	jmp	f3
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

We have 20 case labels, with values between 0 and 87. The compiler could lower this switch to a jump table with 88 entries. Our hypothesis for the heuristic is that a jump table conversion is profitable when its size is smaller than 8 * num_case_labels. Since 88 < 20 * 8, the conversion should be profitable in this case, however gcc opted to lower the switch to a sequence of comparisons.

To better understand why, let's examine a specific block of case labels.

int blocks_2(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
                case 42:  case 43:  case 44:  
        case 45:
            return f3(val);
            }
    return 0;
}

blocks_2:
	mov	eax, edi ; Move `val` to $eax
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 45
	; If val <= 45, do _not_ jump
	jg	.L2
	cmp	eax, 41
	; If val >= 42, jump to L3
	jg	.L3
	; ...
.L2:
; ...
.L3:
        ; We reach L3 only if 42 <= val <= 45
        jmp	f3        ; Call f3(val)
; ...

The compiler realizes that the cases are contiguous and can be implemented with two comparisons instead of four. If the input of the jump table heuristic is the number of comparisons instead of case labels, things work out:

We have a total of 10 comparisons. Since 10 * 8 < 88, our revised heuristic suggests that a jump table transformation is unprofitable.

Non-contiguous

Let us try a non-contiguous case.

int f1(int val);

int bittest(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case '0':  case '2':  case '4':  
        case '5':  case '7':  case '9':  
        case 'A':  case 'C':  case 'E':
            return f1(x);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

bittest:
	lea	eax, [rdi-48]
	cmp	eax, 21
	ja	.L1
	mov	edx, 2753205  ; ???
	bt	rdx, rax
	jc	.L7
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L7:
	jmp	f1

The compiler emits non-intuitive machine code. Why is there no cmp nor jump tables? Where does the constant 2753205 come from?

An hint comes from the instruction bt. According to the Intel docs, bt:

Selects the bit in a bit string (specified with the first operand, called the bit base) at the bit-position designated by the bit offset (specified by the second operand) and stores the value of the bit in the CF flag.

If we examine the binary representation of 2753205, we find that it is in fact a bitset. The bits that are set to one correspond to the ASCII values of the case labels, each value being reduced by 48.

Implementation

We've encountered several distinct lowering strategies employed by gcc. For a more in-depth understanding, we can delve into the compiler's source code.

The compiler pass that responsible for lowering switch statements is the (appropriately named) pass_lower_switch, which in turn calls analyze_switch_statement.

Since gcc source can be daunting to follow, I'll provide a step-by-step commented version below. Following this, I will break down each section to explain its functionality.

bool switch_decision_tree::analyze_switch_statement () 
{
    unsigned l = gimple_switch_num_labels (m_switch);
    auto_vec<cluster *> clusters;
     ...

    compute_cases_per_edge ();

Some preamble code. m_switch points to a gimple object. Gimple is the internal representation used by gcc. Through this, we extract the overall count of cases and the individual counts of cases for each outgoing edge.

We also allocate a vector that will record the lowering strategy chosen for each case label.

    for (unsigned i = 1; i < l; i++)
    {
        tree elt = gimple_switch_label (m_switch, i);
	// ...
        tree low = CASE_LOW (elt);
        tree high = CASE_HIGH (elt);

        profile_probability p
            = case_edge->probability.apply_scale (1, (intptr_t) (case_edge->aux));
        clusters.quick_push (new simple_cluster (low, high, elt, case_edge->dest, p));
        // ...
    }

More setup code. We notice that gimple has a concept of high and low value for each label. That is, contiguous case labels have already joined together at this stage.

For each case label, we allocate a simple_cluster. This cluster serves as a record, capturing the range of values associated with the label, the relevant output edge, and the likelihood of this cluster being chosen. This probability comes from profile-guided optimization. By default it is uniform among case labels.

    // ...
    vec<cluster *> output = bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests (clusters);

We transform the vector of clusters we have created. The name bit_test_cluster hints to the bitset lowering strategy we saw before.

    /* Find jump table clusters.  */
    vec<cluster *> output2;
    auto_vec<cluster *> tmp;
    // ...
    
    for (unsigned i = 0; i < output.length (); i++) {
        cluster *c = output[i];
        if (c->get_type () != SIMPLE_CASE) {
            if (!tmp.is_empty ()) {
                                tmp.truncate (0);
            }
            output2.safe_push (c); 
        }
        else
            tmp.safe_push (c);
    }

This section allocates a vector for the transformed cases and a scratch vector. Any case that wasn't altered during the bitset transformation process is gathered in this scratch vector. These cases are then processed and cleared whenever we come across an optimized cluster.

Essentially, in this section we are looking for sequences of case labels that couldn't be converted into bitset clusters.

                vec<cluster *> n = jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (tmp);
                output2.safe_splice (n);
                n.release ();

We attempt to convert these consecutive labels into a jump table and add the outcome to the output.

    /* We still can have a temporary vector to test.  */
    if (!tmp.is_empty ()) {
        vec<cluster *> n = jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (tmp);
        output2.safe_splice (n);
        n.release ();
    }

This is a coda for the loop above.

    // ...

    bool expanded = try_switch_expansion (output2);
    release_clusters(output2);
    return expanded;
}

Whatever is left goes through another pass, which turns the switch statement into a decision tree. The bitsets and jump table are leaves of the decision tree.

Bitsets

Let's dig further into bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests. The high level structure of the code is as follow.

Initially, we aim to find the optimal method to bundle all clusters into bitsets. Optimality, in this context, refers to minimizing the number of bitsets used. We do so using dynamic programming.

Subsequently, we iterate over the bitsets and apply a profitability heuristic. If the bitsets meet this heuristic, we emit a bit_test_cluster; otherwise, we keep the original simple_clusters.

vec<cluster *> bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests (vec<cluster *> &clusters)
{
     ...

    unsigned l = clusters.length ();
    auto_vec<min_cluster_item> min;
     ...

    min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (0, 0, 0));
    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
            if (min[j].m_count + 1 < min[i].m_count
                    && can_be_handled (clusters, j, i - 1))
                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j, INT_MAX);
        }

        gcc_checking_assert (min[i].m_count != INT_MAX);
    }

For the dynamic programming, we'll use a vector of min_cluster_item structures. Each min_cluster_item has three components:

  • The first records how many bitsets do we need to represent the first i case labels, where i is the index in the vector.
  • The second records the start of the last bitset.
  • The third is unused.

The dynamic programming is as follows. We want to find the minimum number of bitsets to represent the first i case labels.

The base case is straightforward, a single case label can be represented by a single bitset.

Suppose we have already have found the optimal number of bitsets for the first j case label, for all . We define to be the optimal number of splits for the first i elements. This means we already computed , and are now seeking .

If the range of case labels can be represented as a bitset cluster, it must be true that

Conversely, assume we have the optimal assignment for the first i labels. If the last bitset starts at label , this assignment is also optimal when restricted to . Were this not the case, we could improve the assignment on as well.

Therefore, it must be that:

These conditions are exactly what the if statement in the code above checks for.

The can_be_handled function controls whether a range of case labels can be turned into a bitset test. It tests two criteria:

  • The combined range of all the case labels must be smaller than the width of a register. On contemporary systems, the combined range should be less than 64.
  • The case labels must have at most 3 unique outgoing edges.

If there is more than one edge, we emit a cascade of bit tests.

    vec<cluster *> output;
    // ...
    
    /* Find and build the clusters.  */
    for (unsigned end = l;;)
    {
        int start = min[end].m_start;

        if (is_beneficial (clusters, start, end - 1))
        {
            bool entire = start == 0 && end == clusters.length ();
            output.safe_push (new bit_test_cluster (clusters, start, end - 1, entire));
        }
        else
            for (int i = end - 1; i >= start; i--)
                output.safe_push (clusters[i]);

        end = start;

        if (start <= 0)
            break;
    }

    output.reverse ();
    return output;
}

Now we convert only bitsets that satisfy the is_beneficial test. In the code count represents the number of case labels handled by the cluster, while uniq denotes the number of distinct outgoing edges.

bool bit_test_cluster::is_beneficial (unsigned count, unsigned uniq)
{
    return (((uniq == 1 && count >= 3)
              || (uniq == 2 && count >= 5)
              || (uniq == 3 && count >= 6)));
}

Jump tables

The logic for jump table conversion mirrors the one used for bit test conversion. It leverages dynamic programming to identify "clusters" that can be profitably converted to a jump table.

Let's delve into the code. 

vec<cluster *> jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (vec<cluster *> &clusters)
{
    if (!is_enabled ())
        return clusters.copy ();

    unsigned l = clusters.length ();
    auto_vec<min_cluster_item> min;
    min.reserve (l + 1);

We start by preallocating a vector of min_cluster_item. We'll use this vector to keep track of the best jump table assignments for consecutive case clusters.

    min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (0, 0, 0));

We also push the base case for dynamic programming. This corresponds to using a single jump table for the whole switch.

Let's focus now on the main loop.

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio = /* Used in the main heuristic. See next snippet. */;
                
    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        // NOTE(xoranth): Base case
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));
        
        /* Pre-calculate number of comparisons for the clusters.  */
        HOST_WIDE_INT comparison_count = 0;
        for (unsigned k = 0; k <= i - 1; k++)
        {
            simple_cluster *sc = static_cast<simple_cluster *> (clusters[k]);
             NOTE(xoranth): get_comparison_count is 2 for contiguous case 
             labels, and 1 otherwise
            comparison_count += sc->get_comparison_count ();
        }

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
            unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT s = min[j].m_non_jt_cases;
            if (i - j < case_values_threshold ())
                s += i - j;
            
             Prefer clusters with smaller number of numbers covered.  
            if () 
            {
                                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j,
					   s );
            }

            simple_cluster *sc = static_cast<simple_cluster *> (clusters[j]);
            comparison_count -= sc->get_comparison_count ();
        }
    }

The dynamic programming loop mirrors the one we used for bitsets. We want to find the minimum number of jump tables to represent the first i case labels.

We iterate over splits at the j-th case label, for j < i. During each iteration we track the best scoring split. The special case j == 0 represents a single jump table for the entire switch statement.

Inside this inner loop we also keep track of:

  1. How many distinct jump tables we would need to lower the switch.
  2. The start of the last jump table of the decomposition.
  3. How many cases cannot be handled by a jump table. In the code, this is the accumulator s.

Point 1. and 2. are analogous to the bitset lowering pass, while 3. is new and specific to jump tables.

Namely, there is some overhead to dispatching to a jump table, due to the indirect jump and the need to check bounds. Therefore gcc requires a minimum amount of case labels to generate a jump table.

If a split would generate a jump table that is too small, the size of the jump table is added to an accumulator s, which is used as a tie-breaker between different split candidates.

To compute the scoring, we need the comparison count between j-th and the i-th case label. We compute it summing up the number of comparisons for all labels, and decreasing the count as we progress in the inner loop.

We also need the number of unhandled case labels. We determine it comparing the size of the jump table to the result of the case_values_threshold function. This function is architecture dependent and takes into account the presence of switch-case specific instructions, but on modern x64 and Arm64 machines, it defaults to 5.

unsigned int default_case_values_threshold (void) {
    return (targetm.have_casesi () ? 4 : 5);
}

Let's now focus on the main heuristic, starting with how max_ratio is computed. I've reproduced below the main loop, omitting lines unrelated to the main heuristic.

We've seen in the examples section that gcc uses the ratio between jump table entries and comparisons as a metric for the lowering the heuristic. The code below shows that distinct ratios are used when optimizing for speed (flags -O[123|fast]) or size (flag -Os). Specifically, a ratio of 8 is used when optimizing for speed, while a ratio of 2 is used when optimizing for size.

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio
        = (optimize_insn_for_size_p ()
                ? param_jump_table_max_growth_ratio_for_size    // This is `2`
                : param_jump_table_max_growth_ratio_for_speed); // This is `8`

    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        /* Set minimal # of clusters with i-th item to infinite.  */
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));

        // NOTE(xoranth): Compute comparison count, see previous snippet

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
             NOTE(xoranth): Compute unhandled cases, see previous snippet
            
             Prefer clusters with smaller number of numbers covered.  
            if ((min[j].m_count + 1 < min[i].m_count)
               || (min[j].m_count + 1 == min[i].m_count && s < min[i].m_non_jt_cases)
               && can_be_handled (clusters, j, i - 1, max_ratio, comparison_count)) 
            {
                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j,
					   s  );
            }

            // NOTE(xoranth): Update comparison count, see previous snippet
        }
    }

Now onto the main loop. Given two splits, we prefer the one that results in fewer jump tables being emitted. Or, if they would result in the same number of jump tables, we prefer the one that handles the most case labels. We also ignore splits that would result in unprofitable jump tables, where profitability is checked by the can_be_handled function.

The can_be_handled condition, checks for overflow and compares the ratio of case labels to jump table entries:

bool jump_table_cluster::can_be_handled (const vec<cluster *> &clusters,
                                         unsigned start, unsigned end,
                                         unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio,
                                         unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT comparison_count)
{
     If the switch is relatively small such that the cost of one
       indirect jump on the target are higher than the cost of a
       decision tree, go with the decision tree.

       [...]

       For algorithm correctness, jump table for a single case must return
       true.  We bail out in is_beneficial if it's called just for
       a single case.  
    if (start == end)
        return true;

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT range = get_range (clusters[start]->get_low (), clusters[end]->get_high ());
     Check for overflow.  
     ...

    return lhs <= max_ratio * comparison_count;
}

The coda of the function also mirrors the one for bitset clusters. It iterates over all jump tables in reverse order, and prunes the ones that fail the is_beneficial check.

    vec<cluster *> output;
    output.create (4);

    /* Find and build the clusters.  */
    for (unsigned int end = l;;)
    {
        int start = min[end].m_start;

        /* Do not allow clusters with small number of cases.  */
        if (is_beneficial (clusters, start, end - 1))
            output.safe_push (new jump_table_cluster (clusters, start, end - 1));
        else
            for (int i = end - 1; i >= start; i--)
                output.safe_push (clusters[i]);
        end = start;

        if (start <= 0) break;
    }

    output.reverse ();
    return output;
}

The is_beneficial check for jump tables aims to prune small jump tables. It compares the number of case labels to case_values_threshold.

bool jump_table_cluster::is_beneficial (const vec<cluster *> &, unsigned start, unsigned end) {
    if (start == end) return false;
    return end - start + 1 >= case_values_threshold ();
}

Binary tree

If gcc cannot emit a bitset cluster or a jump table, it falls back to a binary tree of comparison.

In emitting the tree, it takes into account the probability of each case label cluster. The probability can be obtained via profile-guided optimization, or with the __builtin_expect_with_probability builtin.

The code is pretty straightforward.

void switch_decision_tree::balance_case_nodes (case_tree_node **head, case_tree_node *parent) 
{
    case_tree_node *np = *head;
    if (np) {
        int i = 0;
        case_tree_node **npp, *left;
        profile_probability prob = profile_probability::never ();

Sum probability of all case labels.

        /* Count the number of entries on branch.  Also count the ranges.  */
        while (np) {
            i++;
            prob += np->m_c->m_prob;
            np = np->m_right;
        }

Split the case label list such that both halves have equal probability.

        if (i > 2) {
            npp = head;
            left = *npp;
	    // NOTE(xoranth): this divides prob by 2.
            profile_probability pivot_prob = prob.apply_scale (1, 2);

            while (1) {
                 Skip nodes while their probability does not reach that amount.  
                prob -= (*npp)->m_c->m_prob;
                if ((prob.initialized_p () && prob < pivot_prob) || ! (*npp)->m_right)
                    break;
                npp = &(*npp)->m_right;
            }

            np = *npp;
            *npp = 0;
            *head = np;
            np->m_parent = parent;
            np->m_left = left == np ? NULL : left;

Recurse in both halves to build the binary tree.

            balance_case_nodes (&np->m_left, np);
            balance_case_nodes (&np->m_right, np);
            np->m_c->m_subtree_prob = np->m_c->m_prob;
            if (np->m_left)
                np->m_c->m_subtree_prob += np->m_left->m_c->m_subtree_prob;
            if (np->m_right)
                np->m_c->m_subtree_prob += np->m_right->m_c->m_subtree_prob;
        } else {
	    // [...] Base case
        }
    }
}

Conclusion

We've seen the heuristics and lowering strategies gcc employs when compiling switch statements, including:

  • Compressing multiple case labels into a bitset.
  • Transforming the switch statement into a jump table.
  • Transforming the switch statement into a binary decision tree.

For anyone interested in delving deeper, I'd suggest examining the gcc source code, and reading this paper.

Finally, I want to thank B.X.V., C.P., and V.P. for their feedback when writing this post

item.description:
